questions.question: What is the empty set?
options: A set whose only element is $0$
A set whose only element is $\varnothing$
A set with exactly one unspecified element

questions.question: Which notation is standard for the empty set?
Which statement correctly distinguishes $\varnothing$ from $\{0\}$?
options: $\varnothing$ has one element, while $\{0\}$ has none.
They are equal because $0$ means nothing.
$\varnothing$ has no elements, while $\{0\}$ has one element.

questions.question: Which set is empty as a subset of $\mathbb R$?
How many elements does $\varnothing$ contain?
Which set is not empty?
Which relation holds between $\varnothing$ and every set $A$?
Why is $\varnothing\subseteq A$ true for every set $A$?
options: Because there is no element of $\varnothing$ that could fail to belong to $A$
Because every set must contain $\varnothing$ as an element, in every case without exception.
Because $A$ must have at least one element
Because $\varnothing$ and $A$ have the same elements

questions.question: How many empty sets are there?
options: There are many different empty sets, one for each universe.
The empty set contains itself as an element by definition.
There is exactly one empty set.
The empty set is equal to every set with cardinality one.

questions.question: What is $A\cup\varnothing$?
What is $A\cap\varnothing$?
Which description correctly captures the empty set?
options: It gives a one-element set used to represent the number zero.
It gives the unique set with no elements and serves as a subset of every set.
It gives the set of all elements not belonging to a chosen set.
It gives a placeholder element that every set must contain.

questions.question: Which of the following is a mistake to avoid when working with the empty set $\varnothing$?
options: Using $\varnothing\subseteq A$ for an arbitrary set $A$
Treating $\varnothing$ and $\{0\}$ as the same set
Using $\varnothing$ to denote the set with no elements

questions.question: What is the power set $\mathcal P(\varnothing)$?
Which statement correctly distinguishes $\varnothing\subseteq A$ from $\varnothing\in A$?
options: $\varnothing\subseteq A$ is always true, but $\varnothing\in A$ depends on $A$.
$\varnothing\in A$ is always true, but $\varnothing\subseteq A$ depends on $A$.
Both are always true for every set $A$.
Both mean exactly the same thing.

questions.question: If $B\subseteq\varnothing$, what must be true?
Which relation between $\varnothing$ and $\{\varnothing\}$ is correct?
Why does the statement “every element of $\varnothing$ has property $P$” count as true?
options: Because there is no element of $\varnothing$ that violates $P$
Because $P$ is automatically true for every object
Because $\varnothing$ contains a hidden element satisfying $P$
Because the statement means that $P$ is false
